title: Genomics, biotechnology and bioinformatics
summary: Reading, copying and editing DNA, and analysing biological data.

layers.basics: Biotechnology uses cells and molecules as tools. PCR copies DNA, gels separate it, sequencers read it, and CRISPR edits it.
layers.deeper: Sequencing a human genome has become more than a hundred thousand times cheaper in two decades, producing datasets that need computing to interpret. Alignment, phylogenetics and omics methods turn raw sequences into biological insight.
layers.expert: Method choice depends on read length, throughput, error profile and cost. Editing technologies raise safety and ethics questions that are as important as the technical ones.

title: Gel electrophoresis
summary: Separating DNA, RNA or proteins by size.

layers.basics: An electric field pulls charged molecules through a gel; smaller pieces move faster, so fragments separate by size.
layers.deeper: DNA is stained (ethidium bromide or safer dyes) and compared to a ladder of known sizes. Agarose is used for DNA, polyacrylamide for proteins and small DNA.
layers.expert: Migration is roughly linear in log10 (size) over a range. Pulsed-field gels separate megabase DNA; capillary electrophoresis underlies automated sequencing.

title: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
summary: Exponentially copying a chosen DNA region.

layers.basics: PCR uses heat cycles, short primers and a heat-stable DNA polymerase to make millions of copies of one DNA segment.
layers.deeper: Each cycle (denature ≈ 95 °C, anneal ≈ 55–65 °C, extend ≈ 72 °C) at best doubles the target. With perfect doubling 30 cycles give 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹ copies; real reactions copy less than perfectly each cycle and level off as reagents run out. Kary Mullis devised it in 1983 (Nobel 1993).
layers.expert: Primer design (Tm, specificity), polymerase fidelity and inhibitors determine success. qPCR measures amplification in real time; RT-PCR starts from RNA; digital PCR counts single molecules.

facts: (1 + E)ⁿ, where E ≤ 1 is the efficiency; 2ⁿ if E = 1

layers.basics: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences; DNA ligase pastes fragments into a vector such as a plasmid.
layers.deeper: Cloned plasmids are put into bacteria (transformation), which copy the DNA as they grow. Antibiotic resistance genes help select the cells that took up the plasmid.
layers.expert: Type II enzymes recognise 4–8 bp palindromes and leave sticky or blunt ends. Modern cloning also uses Gibson assembly and Golden Gate. Blue–white screening uses lacZ to detect inserts.

layers.basics: A gene is put into bacteria, yeast or other cells so they make a human or useful protein, such as insulin.
layers.deeper: Human insulin made in E. coli was approved in 1982. Systems include bacteria, yeast, insect and mammalian cells, chosen by folding and modification needs.
layers.expert: Expression is commonly driven by IPTG-inducible T7 promoters; inclusion bodies, codon bias and missing glycosylation are common problems. Therapeutic antibodies are produced in CHO cells.

layers.basics: A polymerase copies DNA with a few chain-stopping bases that carry fluorescent tags. Fragments ending at each base are sorted by size to read the sequence.
layers.deeper: Reads are up to ≈ 800–1,000 bases with high accuracy (≈ 99.99%). It was used for the Human Genome Project and is still the gold standard for verifying clones.
layers.expert: Capillary arrays read 96 samples in parallel. Read-quality scores (Phred Q = −10 log₁₀P) quantify base-call confidence.

layers.basics: Instead of one fragment at a time, NGS reads millions to billions of short fragments simultaneously, typically 100–300 bases each.
layers.deeper: Illumina sequencing-by-synthesis images fluorescent bases added cycle by cycle. NHGRI's estimate of the production cost of sequencing a human-sized genome fell from ≈ $95 million (2001) to ≈ $525 (2022); the estimate leaves out analysis.
layers.expert: Coverage (reads per base, ≈ 30× for human WGS) determines variant-calling confidence. Long-read platforms (PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore) give 10 kb–Mb reads that resolve repeats and structural variants.

title: Genome assembly and annotation
summary: From reads to a genome and its genes.

layers.basics: Short reads are stitched into longer sequences (assembly) and genes and other features are marked (annotation).
layers.deeper: Repeats make assembly hard. In 2022 the T2T consortium published T2T-CHM13, the first gapless sequence of every human chromosome except Y (3.055 Gb, from a homozygous 46,XX cell line). A gapless Y chromosome followed in 2023.
layers.expert: Assemblers use overlap or de Bruijn graphs; scaffolding uses Hi-C or optical maps. Annotation combines ab initio prediction, RNA-seq evidence and homology.

layers.basics: RNA-seq counts RNA molecules to show which genes are expressed and how much, in a tissue or a single cell.
layers.deeper: Differential expression finds genes that change between conditions. Single-cell RNA-seq reveals cell types and states in a tissue.
layers.expert: Counts are normalised (TPM, DESeq2 size factors) and modelled with negative-binomial statistics. Multiple-testing correction (FDR) is essential when testing ≈ 20,000 genes.

title: Proteomics, metabolomics and systems biology
summary: Measuring whole sets of proteins and metabolites.

layers.basics: Proteomics and metabolomics identify and measure all proteins or small molecules in a sample, mostly using mass spectrometry.
layers.deeper: Combining omics layers with networks gives a systems view of a cell. Biomarker discovery and drug target studies use these methods.
layers.expert: Shotgun proteomics digests proteins and matches peptide spectra to databases; detection of ≈ 10,000 human proteins from one cell line is now routine. Dynamic range of plasma proteins spans ≈ 10 orders of magnitude.

title: CRISPR–Cas9 genome editing

layers.basics: A guide RNA leads the Cas9 enzyme to a matching DNA sequence and cuts both strands. The cell's repair then disrupts or edits the gene.
layers.deeper: CRISPR began as a bacterial immune system against phages. Doudna and Charpentier turned it into a tool in 2012 (Nobel 2020). Casgevy (2023) is the first approved CRISPR therapy, for sickle-cell disease.
layers.expert: Cas9 needs an NGG PAM. Repair by NHEJ makes indels; HDR can insert a template. Off-target cuts, delivery and mosaicism are limits. Base editors and prime editors change bases without double-strand breaks.

did_you_know: The CRISPR repeats were first noticed in E. coli in 1987 and only decades later linked to bacterial immunity.

title: GMOs and transgenic organisms
summary: Organisms with added or edited genes.

layers.basics: Genetically modified organisms carry genes from another species or edited genes. Examples include Bt corn and insulin-producing bacteria.
layers.deeper: Bt crops make a bacterial toxin that kills certain insect pests. Golden Rice is engineered to make beta-carotene. Regulators assess each product for safety and environmental risk.
layers.expert: Meta-analyses find approved GM foods are as safe to eat as conventional ones; environmental questions (gene flow, resistance evolution, herbicide use) are assessed case by case. Gene drives are a distinct, more contested technology.

facts: Share of US corn acres planted with GE varieties (USDA, 2025)

title: Gene therapy and genomic medicine

layers.basics: Gene therapy delivers a working gene or edits a faulty one to treat disease. Viruses are the usual delivery vehicles.
layers.deeper: Approved examples include treatments for SMA, certain inherited blindness, haemophilia and sickle-cell disease. Prices can reach millions of dollars per patient.
layers.expert: AAV vectors have ≈ 4.7 kb capacity and trigger immune responses; lentiviral vectors integrate. Early trials revealed insertional mutagenesis and the 1999 Gelsinger death, shaping oversight.

open_questions: How long do single-dose gene therapies last, and what are their rare long-term risks such as vector integration and immune reactions?
Can very high prices be made sustainable for ultra-rare diseases?

title: DNA profiling and blotting

layers.basics: DNA profiling compares short repeating sequences (STRs) that vary between people. Southern, northern and western blots detect specific DNA, RNA and proteins.
layers.deeper: Forensic profiles use 13–20 STR loci, giving random match probabilities below 1 in a billion. Paternity and identification cases use similar methods.
layers.expert: Match probabilities multiply allele frequencies across loci (product rule), with corrections for relatedness and population structure. Western blots use antibody detection after SDS-PAGE transfer.

facts: well below 1 in 10⁹ for unrelated people; weaker for partial, mixed or related-person comparisons

layers.basics: Alignment lines up two or more DNA or protein sequences to show matches, mismatches and gaps.
layers.deeper: Similarity between sequences suggests common ancestry (homology). Algorithms score matches, mismatches and gap penalties; the best alignment has the highest score.
layers.expert: Needleman–Wunsch (global) and Smith–Waterman (local) dynamic programming are O(mn). Substitution matrices (BLOSUM62, PAM) capture amino-acid exchange. Multiple alignment (Clustal, MAFFT) underlies phylogenetics.

ext.title: Henikoff and Henikoff 1992, PNAS 89:10915: BLOSUM substitution matrices
Needleman and Wunsch 1970, J Mol Biol 48:443

layers.basics: BLAST quickly searches huge databases for sequences similar to yours. Databases like GenBank, UniProt and the PDB store sequences and structures.
layers.deeper: The E-value says how many matches of that score you would expect by chance; smaller is more significant. Annotated databases link sequences to function.
layers.expert: BLAST uses seeds (short words, typically 3 amino acids in protein searches and 11 nucleotides in DNA searches, adjustable by program and settings) extended into high-scoring pairs. GenBank release 274 (October 2026) holds ≈ 9×10¹² bases in its traditional divisions and ≈ 5×10¹³ more in whole-genome-shotgun records; AlphaFold DB provides > 200 million predicted structures.

title: Building phylogenetic trees from data

layers.basics: Trees are built from aligned sequences by distance, parsimony, maximum-likelihood or Bayesian methods.
layers.deeper: Branch lengths show amount of change; bootstrap values (percent) show support. Rooting uses an outgroup.
layers.expert: ML and Bayesian approaches use substitution models (GTR, LG) and rate variation. Molecular clocks calibrated by fossils estimate divergence times. Horizontal gene transfer makes trees of genes differ from the species tree.

facts: Number of rooted trees for n taxa

title: Comparative and human genomics

layers.basics: Comparing genomes shows shared genes between species and what makes each unique. Humans and chimpanzees differ by ≈ 1.2% in single-base changes, plus about five million insertion or deletion events.
layers.deeper: Humans have ≈ 20,000 protein-coding genes, similar to other mammals; only about 5–10% of the genome shows signs of purifying selection (one study: 8.2%, range 7.1–9.2%), and about half is repeat or transposon-derived DNA. How much of the rest is functional is debated. The Human Genome Project (1990–2003) cost ≈ $2.7 billion.
layers.expert: Conserved noncoding elements flag functional regions. Two people differ at about 0.1% of single-base positions, and at least ≈ 0.5% once copy-number and other structural variants are counted. Classic estimates put ≈ 85% of human genetic variation within local populations, so most variation is shared across continents; the exact share depends on the markers and study.

open_questions: How much of the human genome has a biological function, and does the answer depend on how function is defined?

title: Metagenomics and environmental DNA

layers.basics: Sequencing all DNA from a sample (soil, water, gut) reveals the microbes present without growing them.
layers.deeper: 16S rRNA gene sequencing classifies bacteria; shotgun metagenomics adds functional genes. eDNA from water can detect rare animals.
layers.expert: In many environments only a small fraction of the cells seen under a microscope form colonies on standard media (the "great plate count anomaly"); metagenome-assembled genomes expand the tree of life, including Asgard archaea and the CPR bacteria.

facts: Cells that grow on standard media
a small minority in many environments; varies widely by habitat

title: Microbiology and virology
summary: Bacteria, archaea, protists and viruses, and how they affect us.

layers.basics: Microbes are the most numerous and diverse living things. Many are harmless or helpful, a few cause disease, and viruses are particles that replicate only inside cells.
layers.deeper: Bacteria and archaea show enormous metabolic variety, exchange genes horizontally and form communities such as biofilms and the human microbiome. Viruses are classified by their genomes and replication.
layers.expert: Microbial genetics, growth kinetics and ecology link to medicine and the environment: antibiotics, resistance, epidemiology, biogeochemical cycling and biotechnology all depend on them.

layers.basics: Bacteria have a cell wall of peptidoglycan, a nucleoid region, ribosomes, and often flagella or pili.
layers.deeper: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative ones have a thin layer plus an outer membrane. This explains Gram stain results and antibiotic susceptibility.
layers.expert: The outer membrane carries lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin). Capsules, S-layers and endospores add protection; endospores can stay viable for very long times, and revival after millions of years has been claimed (for example from amber and salt crystals) but is not independently established.

title: Microbial growth and culture

layers.basics: Bacteria grow exponentially in a lag, log, stationary and death-phase pattern. They are grown on media with nutrients like agar plates or broth.
layers.deeper: Growth depends on temperature, pH, oxygen and nutrients; organisms are classed as psychrophiles, mesophiles, thermophiles, aerobes, anaerobes and so on.
layers.expert: Exponential growth follows N = N₀·2^(t/g) with generation time g. Selective and differential media (MacConkey, blood agar) help identify species.

facts: ≈ 20 min in optimal lab conditions; longer in poorer conditions

title: Microbial metabolic diversity
summary: Many ways to make a living.

layers.basics: Microbes get energy from light (phototrophs), organic molecules (heterotrophs) or inorganic chemicals (chemolithotrophs), and carbon from CO2 or organic matter.
layers.deeper: Anaerobic respiration uses alternatives to oxygen (nitrate, sulfate, CO2). Cyanobacteria evolved oxygenic photosynthesis at least ≈ 2.4 billion years ago, before the Great Oxidation Event; some evidence points to ≈ 2.7 billion years or earlier, and the date is debated.
layers.expert: Nitrogen fixers (nitrogenase), methanogens, sulfate reducers and anammox bacteria drive global cycles. Electron donors and acceptors set energy yield via the redox tower.

facts: before ≈ 2.4 Ga (≈ 2.7 Ga or earlier debated)
open_questions: When did oxygenic photosynthesis first evolve?

title: Bacterial genetics and horizontal gene transfer

layers.basics: Bacteria share genes by conjugation (plasmid transfer), transformation (taking up free DNA) and transduction (via phage).
layers.deeper: This spreads traits like antibiotic resistance among species. Griffith's 1928 mouse experiments revealed transformation.
layers.expert: Strains of one species can differ widely in gene content (the pan-genome is the set of all genes found in the species). In a 20-strain E. coli study an average genome held ≈ 4,700 genes, the pan-genome held ≈ 17,800, and one strain revealed only about a quarter of it. Integrons, transposons and plasmids (F, R) drive gene mobility; CRISPR provides adaptive defence.

facts: ≈ 2,000 genes in a 20-strain study: ≈ 11% of its 17,838-gene pan-genome, ≈ 40–45% of an average genome

title: Bacterial diversity and phyla

layers.basics: Notable groups include Proteobacteria (E. coli, Salmonella; formally Pseudomonadota), Firmicutes (Bacillus, Streptococcus; formally Bacillota), Actinobacteria (formally Actinomycetota), Cyanobacteria and spirochetes.
layers.deeper: Different groups cause disease, fix nitrogen, make antibiotics (Streptomyces) or photosynthesise (cyanobacteria).
layers.expert: Culture-independent surveys revealed dozens of phyla, including Candidate Phyla Radiation bacteria with tiny genomes. Estimates of how many bacterial and archaeal species exist differ by many orders of magnitude (one scaling-law study predicts up to ≈ 10¹²), while only about 23,000 have validly published names.

open_questions: How many prokaryote species exist, and how should a species be defined?

title: Archaea

layers.basics: Archaea look like bacteria but are genetically closer to eukaryotes. Many live in extreme places, though they also live in soil and oceans.
layers.deeper: Groups include methanogens, halophiles and thermophiles. They have ether-linked membrane lipids and no peptidoglycan.
layers.expert: Asgard archaea contain eukaryote-like proteins and are the closest known relatives of the eukaryotic host (a leading hypothesis). Several archaea grow above 100 °C; Pyrolobus fumarii holds the reproducible record of 113 °C, and Methanopyrus kandleri strain 116 was reported to grow at 122 °C under high pressure (20 MPa) in one study.

facts: ≈ 122 °C under 20 MPa (Methanopyrus kandleri strain 116, one study)
open_questions: Which archaeal lineage gave rise to the eukaryote host cell?

title: Viruses: structure and classification
summary: Genetic material in a protein coat.

layers.basics: A virus is genetic material (DNA or RNA) in a protein shell (capsid), sometimes inside a lipid envelope. It can replicate only within a host cell.
layers.deeper: Shapes include helical, icosahedral and complex. Baltimore classification sorts viruses by genome type and mRNA production (seven classes).
layers.expert: Genomes range from ≈ 1.7 kb (circoviruses) to > 2.5 Mb (pandoraviruses). Whether viruses are alive and how they originated (virus-first, escape, reduction) is unsettled.

open_questions: The origin of viruses (before cells, escaped genes, or reduced cells) remains unresolved and may differ between groups.

layers.basics: A virus attaches to a host receptor, enters, hijacks the cell to copy itself, assembles new particles and leaves.
layers.deeper: In a lytic cycle the virus makes new particles and the cell is destroyed as they are released. In lysogeny the phage genome is kept silently in the host, integrated into its chromosome and copied with it, until a trigger such as stress starts the lytic cycle. Enveloped viruses bud from the membrane.
layers.expert: Burst size, the number of new particles released from one infected cell, varies widely between viruses and conditions. Latency (herpesviruses), antigenic drift (influenza) and reassortment (flu pandemics) are key evolutionary features.

title: Bacteriophages

layers.basics: Bacteriophages are the most abundant biological entities (≈ 10³¹ on Earth). They infect bacteria and can control bacterial populations.
layers.deeper: Phage T4 and λ were model systems that shaped molecular biology. Phage therapy is being revisited for resistant infections.
layers.expert: Phages shuttle genes (transduction), transfer toxins, and shape ocean carbon cycling by an estimated ≈ 20% of the ocean's microorganism biomass killed by viruses each day (a rough, poorly constrained figure). Phage display evolves binding proteins (Nobel 2018).

facts: Ocean microbial biomass killed by viruses/day

layers.basics: Retroviruses like HIV copy their RNA genome into DNA and insert it into the host genome. HIV attacks CD4⁺ T cells and causes AIDS if untreated.
layers.deeper: Antiretroviral drugs target reverse transcriptase, protease and integrase; combination therapy makes HIV a manageable infection. About 41 million people were living with HIV at the end of 2025.
layers.expert: Reverse transcriptase is error-prone (≈ 10⁻⁴ per base) giving rapid evolution and drug resistance. Latent reservoirs in resting cells prevent cure; rare bone-marrow transplants have cured a few patients.

title: Viroids and prions

layers.basics: Viroids are naked circular RNAs that infect plants. Prions are misfolded proteins that convert normal proteins into the misfolded form.
layers.deeper: Prion diseases include mad cow disease (BSE) and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease. They are not destroyed by normal sterilisation.
layers.expert: PrP^Sc seeds conversion of PrP^C; strain diversity is encoded in conformations. Stanley Prusiner received the 1997 Nobel for prion research.

open_questions: What is the high-resolution structure of infectious PrPSc, which form is toxic to neurons, and what encodes strain differences?

title: Emerging viruses and pandemics
summary: Where new viral threats come from.

layers.basics: New viruses often jump from animals to people (zoonosis). Examples are HIV, influenza, Ebola and SARS-CoV-2.
layers.deeper: Mutation, reassortment and recombination give variants. Surveillance, vaccines and antivirals are the main responses.
layers.expert: R₀ and generation time drive spread; COVID-19 (first detected in 2019; WHO ended its international emergency status on 5 May 2023) has about 7.1 million officially reported deaths, and WHO estimated ≈ 14.8 million excess deaths in 2020 and 2021 alone, so the true toll is higher than the reported count. Origin investigations weigh zoonotic spillover against lab-related hypotheses; this remains debated for SARS-CoV-2.

open_questions: The precise origin of SARS-CoV-2 has not been conclusively established.

title: Protists
summary: Diverse eukaryotes that are not plants, animals or fungi.

layers.basics: Protists are mostly single-celled eukaryotes: amoebas, ciliates, algae, diatoms and parasites like Plasmodium.
layers.deeper: They include producers, predators and parasites. Diatoms and dinoflagellates are important marine photosynthesisers, and malaria kills ≈ 600,000 people a year.
layers.expert: Protists are not a natural group: they are the eukaryotes left over once animals, plants and fungi are set aside, and they are spread across several supergroups (Opisthokonta, which also holds animals and fungi, Archaeplastida, SAR, Excavata, Amoebozoa). Secondary endosymbiosis shaped plastids of many algae.

facts: ≈ 20% of global, up to ≈ 40% of marine (estimates)

title: Human microbiome
summary: Microbes living on and in us.

layers.basics: Trillions of microbes live in the gut, on the skin and elsewhere. Most are harmless or helpful, aiding digestion and training immunity.
layers.deeper: Gut bacteria make vitamins and short-chain fatty acids. Antibiotics, diet and early life shape the community; imbalance (dysbiosis) is linked with disease.
layers.expert: Human cells and bacteria are roughly 1:1 (≈ 3.8×10¹³ bacteria). Causation versus correlation in microbiome–disease links is still being tested, and fecal transplants are approved for recurrent C. difficile.

facts: Microbial genes in a gut catalogue
3.3 million (2010, 124 people); the count grows with sampling
open_questions: Which microbiome–disease associations are causal (versus consequences) is still mostly unresolved.

title: Pathogenesis and virulence

layers.basics: A pathogen must reach the host, attach, evade defences and damage tissue. Toxins, enzymes and capsules help.
layers.deeper: Exotoxins (cholera, botulinum) are proteins; endotoxin is LPS from Gram-negative walls. Koch's postulates link a microbe to a disease.
layers.expert: Virulence factors are often on pathogenicity islands or plasmids. ID50 (infectious dose) and LD50 quantify virulence; botulinum toxin is among the most lethal known (estimated human lethal dose ≈ 1–2 ng/kg by injection; other routes differ).

facts: ≈ 1–2 ng/kg by injection (0.09–0.15 µg for 70 kg)

title: Antibiotics: mechanisms and discovery
summary: Drugs that kill or stop bacteria.

layers.basics: Antibiotics target bacterial structures absent from human cells: cell wall synthesis (penicillin), ribosomes, DNA gyrase or folate synthesis.
layers.deeper: Fleming noticed in 1928 that a Penicillium mould killed bacteria on a plate. Florey, Chain and colleagues later purified penicillin and showed it worked in patients, in the early 1940s. Antibiotics act on bacterial targets, so they do nothing against viruses.
layers.expert: Selective toxicity depends on target differences (70S vs 80S ribosomes). Spectrum, MIC and pharmacokinetics guide use; many antibiotics derive from soil actinomycetes.

title: Antibiotic resistance

layers.basics: Bacteria evolve resistance when exposed to antibiotics. The sensitive ones die and the resistant ones multiply.
layers.deeper: Mechanisms: drug inactivation (β-lactamases), altered targets, efflux pumps and reduced uptake. Misuse in medicine and farming speeds resistance.
layers.expert: AMR was associated with ≈ 4.7 million deaths in 2021 (≈ 1.1 million directly attributable). MRSA, CRE and drug-resistant TB are priority threats; new classes are rare, so stewardship, phage therapy and diagnostics matter.

facts: only a handful (e.g. oxazolidinones, cyclic lipopeptides); 12 classes were launched 1935–1968

layers.basics: Heat, filtration, radiation and chemicals kill or remove microbes. Sterilisation kills all life; disinfection reduces pathogens.
layers.deeper: An autoclave uses steam at 121 °C and 15 psi for ≈ 15–20 minutes. Alcohol (70%) works better than 100% on many bacteria.
layers.expert: D-value and Z-value describe thermal death kinetics; endospores and prions need harsher treatment. Efficacy tests include the phenol coefficient and disk diffusion.

layers.basics: Microbes stick to surfaces inside a slimy matrix (biofilm) and use chemical signals (quorum sensing) to coordinate when they are numerous.
layers.deeper: Biofilms on teeth (plaque) and catheters resist antibiotics and immune cells. Vibrio fischeri's glow in squid is the classic quorum example.
layers.expert: Biofilm cells can tolerate 10–1,000× higher antibiotic doses. Signals include AHLs (Gram-negatives) and peptides (Gram-positives).
